content: A mucocele, also known as a mucus extravasation phenomenon, is a swelling of connective tissue caused by the accumulation of mucin that leaks from a ruptured salivary gland duct. This condition is most commonly triggered by local trauma. Mucoceles typically present as bluish, translucent swellings and are more frequently observed in children and young adults. The most common site for a mucocele is the surface of the lower lip. However, they can also occur on the inner side of the cheek (referred to as the buccal mucosa), the anterior ventral surface of the tongue, and the floor of the mouth. When located on the floor of the mouth, the lesion is specifically termed a ranula. Mucoceles are rarely found on the upper lip. The size of mucoceles can range from as small as 1 millimeter to several centimeters. On palpation, they may feel fluctuant, but in some cases, they can be firm. Their duration can vary significantly, lasting from a few days to several years. Mucoceles may exhibit recurrent swelling and can occasionally rupture, releasing their contents. A variant of the mucocele, known as a superficial mucocele, can be found on the palate, retromolar pad, and posterior buccal mucosa. This type appears as single or multiple vesicles that eventually rupture, forming an ulcer. Although these lesions heal within a few days, they often recur in the same location. Microscopically, mucoceles are characterized by granulation tissue surrounding pools of mucin. Inflammatory cells, such as neutrophils and foamy histiocytes, are typically present due to the concurrent inflammatory response. Some mucoceles resolve spontaneously within a short period. However, chronic mucoceles often require surgical intervention for removal. Recurrence is possible, and to prevent this, the adjacent salivary gland is often excised. Various surgical techniques are available for the removal of mucoceles, including laser and minimally invasive procedures, which significantly reduce recovery times.
